claim: A working-memory load cuts relational (structure-based) mapping in humans and pushes answers to attribute matches. Verbal 7-digit load: .35 vs .64 (N=45); phonological and executive loads: .24 vs .45 (N=109). Anxiety (an executive drain) gives the same shift (45% vs 68%, N=22).
schema_part: G/S mapping stage; O (map) - keep mapping steps small
agent_test: Same analogy items with a filler-heavy vs trimmed context at equal tokens; score relational vs attribute matches.

claim: The two loads (phonological repetition vs random-digit generation) hurt equally, so human data do not separate storage from executive control as the bottleneck.
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM directly; skip.

claim: Asking for several mappings at once (3 objects) raises relational mappings in humans, from .39 to .60 (Exp 1) and .25 to .37 (Exp 2), with no interaction with load. No LLM test of joint vs single-pair mapping prompts was found (gap 4 open).
schema_part: O (map) - ask for a global mapping, not one pair
agent_test: A/B: single-pair vs joint-mapping prompt on cross-mapped pairs at equal tokens.

claim: Human core working-memory capacity is about 3 to 5 chunks, not 7; chunking and blocked rehearsal decide the number.
agent_test: Cap items per reasoning step at 3-4 and compare with uncapped at equal tokens.

claim: Training human working memory does not transfer to analogy: large gains on trained tasks (d=1.9 to 3.2) and none on verbal analogy (d=0.10) or visual analogy (d=0.05).
agent_test: Weakens the causal story; for an LLM, extra memory tools may help the task without improving analogy itself. Compare tool vs no tool.

claim: The causal link from working memory to analogy is contested: capacity-count accounts (relational complexity, LISA) compete with binding quality (Chuderski) and inhibition (Richland, DORA) accounts.
agent_test: Compare prompts that limit relation count vs prompts that force explicit role-filler tables; see which helps more.

claim: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates zero-shot on digit matrices (OR 1.88 generative, 6.27 multiple choice, N=40) and showed human-like difficulty by rule count (item-level r=0.39).
agent_test: Baseline only; re-run on current models.

claim: Difficulty rising with number of distinct rules (a working-memory signature) appears in both humans (OR 0.41) and GPT-3 (OR 0.07), yet this is not proof of a human-like bottleneck.
agent_test: Vary distinct-relation count at fixed length; find where accuracy breaks for our agent.

claim: The letter-string claim of general analogy is contested: GPT-3 collapses on shuffled alphabets (generative accuracy <0.1 on 4 of 6 types) and Lewis and Mitchell found humans .753 vs GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452.
agent_test: Run counterfactual letter-string items on our agent with and without code at equal tokens.

claim: The counterfactual failure is largely a counting and position failure: GPT-4 with code execution matched humans (P=0.496) while plain GPT-4 stayed worse (P=8.9e-13); 46% of GPT-4 errors were valid alternative rules vs 39% for humans.
agent_test: Give agent a code tool for symbol counting vs none at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs show an n-back capacity limit: d' falls to about 1 at 3-back for gpt-3.5-turbo; noise lowers it; chain-of-thought helps; GPT-4 is far above small open models.
agent_test: n-back style item tracking with scratchpad vs without at equal tokens.

claim: Scale alone does not remove working-memory limits: across 7 OpenAI models n-back stayed below human level; advanced prompts help big models (BBH cat. ii GPT-3.5 44.4 to 67.6) and can hurt small ones.
agent_test: Check structured prompts vs answer-only on our model size.

claim: Prompting the model to write its own related examples before solving gives gains over 0-shot and manual few-shot CoT (GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.0 to 77.8; MATH 33.0 to 37.3; text-davinci-003 14.8 to 61.0).
agent_test: Self-generated analog step vs none at equal tokens (count the generation cost).

claim: Advanced LLMs match humans on semantic structure-mapping in some conditions but diverge under semantic distractors (distracted condition about -0.25 for all).
agent_test: Insert irrelevant but similar content in analogy items; measure drop.

claim: Newer models do well on simple relations but weaker on analogy in a preregistered nonword battery (GPT OSS 120B 99.8% same/different, about 83% analogy; Llama near chance on analogy); premise count 1 to 5 barely hurt comparative relations.
agent_test: Run the nonword battery on our agent.

claim: Relational-bottleneck architectures (ESBN, Slot Abstractors) generalise out of distribution by forcing separate binding memory (95%+ rule generalisation; V-PROM 67.7 vs 51.2).
agent_test: Analogue in scaffold: explicit variable-binding table as external memory.

claim: Serial incremental mapping (IAM, Keane and Brayshaw 1988) is supported by one human order effect and one similarity effect in Keane, Ledgeway, Duff 1994: Singleton-First 178.0 s vs Singleton-Last 363.1 s (N=20); similarity 210.9, 164.9, 69.7 s (N=21). LISA and relational-complexity claims remain unopened.
agent_test: Shuffle base-item order in analogy prompts and check whether accuracy changes.

claim: Reasoning models do not remove the analogy and load limits: o3-mini fell 86.6% to 17.0% and R1 80.6% to 23.2% on longer, noisier Raven-style items despite 3.4x more reasoning tokens; late-2025 frontier models stay below humans on far-analogy grid tasks (best 10.13 points under humans, strict).
agent_test: Test our agent on long, noisy relational items.

claim: Irrelevant context and sheer input length hurt LLM reasoning: under 30% of math problems stay consistently solved after one distractor sentence; accuracy falls 0.92 to 0.68 from 250 to 3000 tokens with the task fixed. This parallels the human attribute-match shift, but no study ran it on analogy mapping scored for relational vs attribute answers.
agent_test: Equal-token A/B of filler-heavy vs trimmed context on analogy items.

claim: Answer-order and position sensitivity: GPT-4 is right 89% when the correct story is first and 61% when second; humans show none (78% both). Moving the blank in digit matrices drops GPT from about .81 to .48. Order effects are also the IAM signature in humans (178.0 vs 363.1 s).
agent_test: Run each analogy item with candidates and base items in two orders and compare.

claim: No test was found of an LLM with a cap on mapping size (3 to 4 relations per step) vs unrestricted at equal tokens. Nearest evidence is operand count in I-RAVEN-X, where LLMs fall from 59.3% to 4.4% arithmetic accuracy and reasoning models from 80.5% to 63.0%.
agent_test: Run the cap test ourselves; it is an open experiment.

claim: Models carry an internal binding mechanism (binding ID vectors; over 97% accuracy when entity and attribute interventions cancel). Whether an explicit external role-filler table beats a relation-count cap for analogy accuracy is untested.
agent_test: Compare binding-table prompt vs count-cap prompt vs plain at equal tokens.

claim: The token-cost question for structured prompts is unanswered: Yasunaga 2024 states it uses more output tokens and reports no equal-token comparison; its self-consistency variant adds more samples (GSM8K 77.8 to 85.3).
agent_test: Match total tokens against a plain longer chain of thought.

claim: No independent larger-N replication of Waltz 2000 or of Tohill and Holyoak 2000 was found. Related human work (relational matching under load 2019; sources of distraction 2022) points the same way but is not a replication and was seen as abstracts only.
agent_test: Treat the human load effect as one lab's result.
